Regarding Xbox

In June 2026 we announced that the release of Big Walk would be limited to computers, Switch 2 and PS5. Since then, we have received many messages and comments, asking about a future Xbox release. We would like to address those questions here:

We have made the decision not to release Big Walk on Xbox, in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement’s call to boycott Microsoft, and their designation of Microsoft Games (and Xbox) as a priority boycott target. If you need help understanding our motives, we would recommend reading about why Microsoft is a BDS priority target, the successes this kind of pressure has already had on Microsoft, and especially, watching this great introductory piece by People Make Games.

It has always been our intention for Big Walk to be played by groups of friends, and we know that keeping the game off Xbox runs counter to those intentions. We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets.

We’ve made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free.

Thank you for your understanding.

Sincerely,
House House

AWS Security Hub CSPM (https://aws.amazon.com/security-hub/) now supports automated security checks that align with the Cyber Risk Institute (CRI) profile. The CRI Profile is a cybersecurity framework developed by the Cyber Risk Institute, a non-profit coalition of financial institutions and trade associations. The framework harmonizes cybersecurity and regulatory expectations that apply to the financial services sector into a common set of requirements, so that an organization can assess itself once and report against multiple regulations. AWS Security Hub CSPM provides 404 controls that support a subset of CRI Profile v2.2 requirements; the controls don't support requirements that require manual checks.


The new standard is now available in all AWS Regions where Security Hub CSPM is currently available, including the AWS GovCloud (US) and the China Regions. To quickly enable the standard across your AWS environment, we recommend that you use Security Hub central configuration. With this approach, you can enable the standard in all or only some of your organization's accounts and across all AWS Regions that are linked to Security Hub with a single action.


To learn more, see CRI Profile v2.2 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/standards-reference-cri-profile.html) in the AWS Security Hub CSPM user guide. To receive notifications about new Security Hub CSPM features and controls subscribe to the Security Hub SNS topic (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/securityhub-announcements.html). You can also try Security Hub CSPM at no cost for 30 days (https://aws.amazon.com/security-hub/cspm/pricing/) with the AWS Free Tier offering.
external.title: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports the Cyber Risk Institute profile version 2.2

OpenAI lets anyone inject ads into ChatGPT users’ sessions, targeting specific groups of people based on their email address, phone number, or a unique identifier on their phone, according to 404 Media’s own tests of ChatGPT’s advertising ecosystem.
While the ad targeting available in ChatGPT is somewhat standard practice across the advertising industry, the chatbot’s one billion monthly active users may not understand they, in some cases, are being specifically targeted because of their personal data the advertiser has uploaded to OpenAI. ChatGPT’s ad targeting is also novel in that it is also based on the prompts users enter into the chatbot, prompts that users may assume are private but which, as 404 Media has previously shown, may be reviewed by humans. Or in this case, used for ad targeting purposes.

Regular 404 Media readers will know about realtime bidding — the near instantaneous process that happens when a company tries to place an ad in front of you — and how spy firms exploit that to extract phones’ location data. Well, another way ads can be exploited is by using them to deliver malware. This used to be a really big problem around ten years ago (wow, check out this WIRED piece I wrote about the issue in 2015!). That was kinda boring, lowgrade criminal malware though. This new research is about ads delivering mobile phone spyware — think in the same vein as NSO Group, which can exfiltrate essentially all sensitive data from a fully up to date mobile phone. That’s nuts both because of the potency of the malware, but also that delivering malware like this could target many, many more people than a direct iMessage attack or similar.

"A young male house finch perches on a curved black metal bar, looking very much like he’s still waking up. His feathers are slightly tousled, giving him that unmistakable “first thing in the morning” look. The reddish wash on his chest is soft and uneven, as if the color hasn’t quite settled in yet — the kind of patchy blush young males often have before they mature into their full, bright plumage.

His beak is thick and conical, a sturdy little tool that seems oversized compared to his sleepy expression. The finch’s eyes are half‑alert, half‑dreamy, as though he’s trying to remember whether he meant to be up this early. His claws grip the bar with casual steadiness, but his posture has that relaxed, slightly rumpled feel of a bird that hasn’t fully committed to the day.

Behind him, the background melts into a soft blur of muted color, making his messy feathers and gentle red tones stand out even more. record.text: Nor is this some new-fangled idea - you'll find it back in the 1947 Truman Commission Report on Higher Education (screen-shotted below), produced by those wild-eyed idealists who had just finished ::checks notes:: the Second World War.

images.alt:
"The net result of the situation is that the college student is faced with a bewildering array of intensive courses from which to make up his individual program. To secure a reasonably comprehensive grasp of his major field, he must in some cases spend as much as half or more of his time in that one department. The other half he scatters among courses in other departments which, designed for future specialists in those fields, are so restricted in scope that the student can gain from them only a fragmentary view of the subject. He, therefore, leaves college unacquainted with some of the fundamental areas of human knowledge and without the integrated view of human experience that is essential both for personal balance and for social wisdom.
Today's college graduate may have gained technical or professional training in one field of work or another, but is only incidentally, if at all, made ready for performing his duties as a man, a parent, and a citizen. Too often he is "educated" in that he has acquired competence in some particular occupation, yet falls short of that human wholeness and civic conscience which the cooperative activities of citizenship require.
The failure to provide any core of unity in the essential diversity of higher education is a cause for grave concern. A society whose numbers lack a body of common experience and common knowledge is a society without a fundamental culture; it tends to disintegrate into a mere aggregation of individuals. Some community of values, ideas, and attitudes is essential as a cohesive force in this age of minute division of labor and intense conflict of special interests.
The crucial task of higher education today, therefore, is to provide a unified general education for American youth. Colleges must find the right relationship between specialized training on the one hand, aiming at a thousand different careers, and the transmission of a common cultural heritage toward a common citizenship on the other. "
